p: I have described the printing press as the invention which multiplied the voice of every man. The men of the future have made an invention which, by their own account, has multiplied it again a millionfold, and has placed in the hands of nearly every person on earth a library, a post office, a newspaper, a market, a theatre and a public meeting, all at once, and all in a small slab of glass. They call it the internet, a word made from the Latin inter, meaning between, and the English net, because it is a network of networks. It is, I must confess, the invention whose history I have found hardest to understand, for its parts are invisible, and its workings are carried on by the calculating machines of which I spoke before, talking to one another in a language of numbers far too fast for any human ear. I shall describe its history as plainly as I can.

It began, like a good many inventions of the twentieth century, with the military fears of the Cold War, though its builders were mostly academic men with very unmilitary habits. In the nineteen-sixties, the American defence department paid for research into ways of linking the calculating machines of different universities, so that scientists could share them. A notion developed independently by an American, Paul Baran, and by an Englishman at the National Physical Laboratory, Donald Davies, proved decisive: that a message, instead of being sent along a single fixed line like a telegram or a telephone call, could be cut into small pieces, called packets, each labelled with its destination, and sent separately by whatever route happened to be free, to be reassembled at the other end. Such a network would have no centre and could survive the destruction of any part of it.

On the twenty-ninth of October, nineteen sixty-nine, a student at the University of California in Los Angeles tried to send the word login to a machine at the Stanford Research Institute, some three hundred and fifty miles away, on this new network, called the ARPANET, from the initials of the agency that paid for it. The receiving machine crashed after receiving the first two letters, l and o. So the first message ever sent on the ancestor of the internet was lo, as in lo and behold. I find that a very satisfactory beginning, worthy of the King James Bible.

In the nineteen-seventies, two Americans, Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn, devised a common set of rules, or protocols, by which networks of different kinds could pass packets to one another, and on the first of January, nineteen eighty-three, the ARPANET adopted them. That is often given as the birthday of the internet. For its first twenty years it was used chiefly by scientists and universities, for sending messages, called electronic mail, and for exchanging files. It was a quiet, scholarly place, rather like a college common room, and many of its early users remember it fondly for that reason.

The internet became the thing that the whole world uses through the invention of an Englishman, Tim Berners-Lee, working at a great European laboratory for physics near Geneva, called CERN. In nineteen eighty-nine, wishing to help the physicists there to share their documents, he proposed a system by which any document on any machine could contain links to any other, so that a reader could pass from one to the next with a touch. He called it the World Wide Web. He wrote the first program for reading it, and the first program for serving it, and, crucially, his laboratory gave the whole invention away freely, without patent or fee, in nineteen ninety-three. Within a few years there were millions of these linked pages, and then billions.

There followed, in quick succession, things that I can describe only by their effects. Great companies arose to search the web for anything a person might want to know, and to sell advertising beside the answers. Shops opened that existed only on the web, and the bookseller and the draper of every high street found their trade drained away. Newspapers lost their readers to free sources of news, of very various reliability. People began to keep up their friendships, and their quarrels, through what are called social networks, on which anyone may publish anything to anyone, instantly. From about two thousand and seven, the telephone, now carried in the pocket and connected to the internet without wires, became the chief means by which most people reached it. The Encyclopaedia reports that by the twenty-twenties, some two-thirds of the people of the earth were using the internet. The Encyclopaedia itself, I should add, is a creature of the web: written, as I have said, by countless unpaid volunteers, and free to every reader. It is the most extraordinary act of collective scholarship in the history of the world, and I do not say that lightly.

For persons who cannot see, I learn, the machines of the future will read aloud any page of the web, by an artificial voice; there are persons, deprived of sight, who listen to whole libraries in this way and can converse with the world as freely as anyone. For the scholar in a remote country, the patient with a rare disease, the young person in a small town who feels alone in the world, the web has opened doors that were locked to every previous generation. Knowledge that was once confined to a few great libraries is available to anyone. I should like to have had it when I was writing my first book, which required three journeys to the Bodleian, one to Paris and a long correspondence with a canon of Toledo who never answered.

But the Encyclopaedia is candid about the darker side. Falsehoods spread on the web faster than truth, because falsehoods are often more exciting. The great companies that control the web gather information about the habits and opinions of their users on a scale that no secret police of the past could have dreamed of, and use it to sell them things and to keep their attention. Governments use the same methods to watch their subjects. The quarrels of nations and parties are inflamed by it. The young are said to spend many hours a day staring at their little glass slabs, which their elders deplore, as the elders of my own youth deplored novels.

I said of the printing press that its enthusiasts should first read the history of the hundred years of religious war that followed it. I say the same of the internet. Every great enlargement of the human voice has amplified our wisdom and our folly together. The press gave us both the Bible in English and the scurrilous pamphlet; the internet gives us both the Encyclopaedia and its opposite. Which will prevail is not a question that the machines can answer. It depends, as it always has, on the character of the people who use them.
